osfacts — scoped, honest OS process & socket facts

Features·budding·accepted·JUL 27, 2026

A standalone Rust tool — one versioned snapshot of processes and sockets, scoped to the ask and honest about what it couldn't read — shipped into kolu's port sensor, with drishti's full migration as the remaining arc.

Contents

  • The contract
  • Why not an existing tool
  • Adoption — kolu and drishti
    • The phase tree — track prefix OSF

osfacts is a product of its own — its own README, its own CI, its own repo-to-be — not a kolu module. One static Rust binary that answers what does the OS say about these processes and their sockets, scoped to exactly what you asked, honest about what it could not read, in about ten milliseconds. The binary and kolu’s port-sensor adoption shipped in #1996; drishti’s adoption attempt (srid/drishti#122) is what wrote the rest of the phase tree below.Every measurement in this note comes from the #1982 candidate sweep — the note is where that week’s conclusions live on after the scratchpads that produced them are gone.

The creed, one line per word — also the repo README’s opening:

  • Scoped — cost tracks the ask (--roots walks a subtree), never the host.
  • Attributed — every snapshot carries the full pid→ppid table, so a grandchild listener walks back to its root.
  • Honest — what it could not read is reported, never silently dropped.
  • Versioned — schema version first; a mismatched consumer fails loudly instead of parsing a half-understood shape into zero rows.
  • Fast — ~10 ms per snapshot, because interactive callers poll at seconds scale. This budget is the requirement that explains every rejection in the comparison table.

The contract

One verb, composable facets, first-class scoping — every user story is the same verb with different facets, never a consumer-shaped flag or mode:

who wants to know runs comes back
kolu’s port sensor, every ~5 s which ports this terminal’s subtree listens on osfacts snapshot --roots 4242 --procs --ports pid table + listener rows with raw addresses; unreadable pids listed, so a blind terminal renders blind, not empty
drishti’s inspector the process tree under a service, with memory and age osfacts snapshot --roots 991 --procs --mem --start-time one row per descendant with RSS and start time
kolu’s daemon supervisor is this pid still mine, and since when osfacts snapshot --pids 991 --start-time a start time to compare against the recorded one
padi’s socket takeover which pids hold this unix socket osfacts socket-holders /run/user/1000/padi.sock the holder pids, or none
drishti’s host dashboard how the machine itself is doing osfacts host --cpu --mem --load --net --disk cumulative counters + gauges, one versioned schema
a human at any shell all of it, readable osfacts snapshot --json | jq the same facts as JSON
  • Scoping is the headline. --roots walks the given pids’ subtrees, --pids takes an exact set, no flag means host-wide. Cost then tracks the ask, not the host — the property no surveyed tool has and the one the measurements say matters most.
  • Facets so a consumer pays only for what it reads: --procs, --ports, --mem, --start-time. socket-holders and host are separate verbs because they answer different questions (a path, not a pid set; the machine, not a process).
  • One versioned schema. TSV on the hot path (V<TAB>1 first, tagged rows), --json for humans and one-offs.
  • Raw address bytes, never a wildcard boolean. Consumers keep exactly one classifier. Two predicates that must agree about ::ffff:0.0.0.0 is precisely how they come to disagree.
  • Cumulative counters, never rates. CPU% and bytes/s are consumer-side diffs between two snapshots; a one-shot sampler never sleeps.This is why procs costs ~30 ms even at its lowest setting: it sleeps to compute a rate nobody asked it for.
  • A MANDATORY unreadable section. Every pid that could not be inspected is reported, with its errno — the policy of what is fatal stays in the consumer, the only layer that knows which pids it asked about.The sudo lesson made structural: when an unreadable pid was silently dropped, one sudo password prompt emptied the Ports section for every terminal on the host; when it threw indiscriminately, one foreign-uid descendant did the same.

Why not an existing tool

Every candidate was measured, not surveyed, and each fails on the contract above rather than on packaging — a packaging gap is an errand, not an architecture verdict.Earlier drafts listed “not packaged for darwin” against osquery and “not in nixpkgs” against portls. Both struck: anything merely absent from nixpkgs could be packaged in an afternoon, so packaging never counts as a disqualifier. The repo README carries this same table:

candidate disqualifier
osquery the wrong operational model: a resident fleet-telemetry agent with a SQL surface, measured at ~378 ms per query and ~158 MB — built for querying thousands of machines every few minutes, not one machine every five seconds on a 10 ms budget
procs discards the bind address — loopback and wildcard collapse to one row
portls no PPID, no process table — a listener cannot be walked back to its root
rustnet interactive capture TUI, needs packet-capture privilege
portview listener rows only, no process table — a shell → npm → node server cannot be walked back to its terminal. No subtree scoping either: its single-port query is a host-wide scan plus a filterportview is also the strongest evidence for building this: it measures 9.9 ms on darwin against our former C helper’s 10.6 ms on the same box by the same method, in Rust, in a single pass. Single-pass Rust matches C — the language was never the constraint, the double enumeration was. That measurement is what settled osfacts on Rust.
sysinfo+listeners wrapping the two crates enumerates the process list twice: 23 ms darwin / ~100 ms linux against 10 ms for a single pass — and listeners shipped the v4-mapped decode bug we fixed upstreamThe ~50-line darwin address decode from that fix is vendored into osfacts with its regression fixtures; upstream is pinned in CI as a drift oracle. The repo README’s Testing section owns the detail.
lsof / netstat lsof measured 93 ms; macOS netstat is intermittently blind — success and zero rows in one sampling window, 29 rows in the next, same boot

Adoption — kolu and drishti

Inside kolu the OS used to be inspected in five places, each with its own hand-rolled reader, its own error policy, and its own platform split — five answers to one question. All five collapse into calls to the one binary, and a full-source sweep confirmed the list is exhaustive.The sweep covered every package including @kolu/surface. The one near-miss: surface-remote’s groupAlive probe (process.kill(-pid, 0) — process-group liveness inside a SIGTERM→SIGKILL escalation timer). Deliberately not a consumer: group liveness is not in the fact set, and forking a snapshot binary inside an escalation timer is the wrong operational model.

consumer asks path
padi port scan a subtree’s processes + listening ports shipped — osfacts-client (OSF2, #1996); the C helper, TS /proc readers and @kolu/port-scan deleted
padi memorySampler per-pid RSS OSF3 — today only self-measurement plus an RPC hop to kaval
daemon supervisor “is this pid still ours”, and since when OSF3 — today kill(pid, 0) liveness only
socketHolder (in surface-daemon-supervisor) which pids hold a unix socket path OSF4 — today /proc/net/unix + fd readlinks; darwin lsof
drishti process inspection + host telemetry OSF3 · OSF6 · OSF7 — first attempt srid/drishti#122

Drishti’s first adoption attempt hit two walls, and they name the missing phases. srid/drishti#122 moved process identity and listeners onto the contract, then deployment as an ordinary SSH user turned red: 41 system processes came back readable as P rows but U … EACCES for their fds, so every one of them rendered listener-blind — honest, but useless for a whole-host inspector (OSF6). And srid/drishti#123 inventories the native host-telemetry readers the contract doesn’t cover at all — /proc gauges, vm_stat, sysctl, netstat -ib, Node os calls, statfs (OSF7).

The phase tree — track prefix OSF

phase delivers needs
OSF1 — the binary snapshot --roots --procs --ports on both platforms · versioned TSV + --json · the mandatory unreadable section · the scar-tissue suite — shipped in #1996 —
OSF2 — kolu’s port sensor padi invokes the baked osfacts binary through osfacts-client; C helper, TS /proc, and @kolu/port-scan deleted — shipped in #1996 OSF1
OSF3 — memory & age facets --mem + --start-time: kolu’s memorySampler gains a true per-pid read and the supervisor gains start-time identity; drishti’s process detail gains RSS and age (absent from #122 by contract, never fabricated) — shipped in #2011 OSF1
OSF4 — socket-holders the second verb ships; socketHolder deletes its /proc/net/unix and lsof paths OSF1
OSF6 — unattributed listeners a listener no readable pid claims is emitted with explicit unattributed status (and its owning uid on linux) instead of dropped — the fix for #122’s privilege regression — shipped in #2011Linux already parses the world-readable /proc/net/tcp{,6} table — address, port, uid, inode — and today discards any LISTEN row no scoped fd readlink claims; emitting it is honesty, not new privilege. Two points the phase must pin: under a narrow --roots, an unclaimed socket may simply belong to an out-of-scope process, so the row says unclaimed, never unowned; and darwin’s only fd-walk-free enumeration is the pcblist sysctl behind netstat — the source measured intermittently blind — so the silent-empty detection scar rides this phase. OSF1
OSF7 — host facets the host verb: load, memory + swap, uptime, per-core cumulative CPU, per-interface cumulative counters, root-fs capacity — drishti deletes its native telemetry readers (srid/drishti#123) — shipped in #2011Semantics to preserve, per the issue: cache-aware available memory, swap used/total, cumulative per-interface byte counters, per-core CPU deltas. Cumulative per the creed — rates are consumer-side diffs between snapshots; the tool never sleeps. OSF1
OSF5 — drishti & extraction drishti’s migration relands whole — every native reader deleted, fail-fast baked path — and the directory graduates to its own repoThe directory moves wholesale: osfacts/ already carries its own README, default.nix, a zero-input subflake, and client-ts/ (osfacts-client — no @kolu scope, Node builtins only) precisely so extraction is a move, not a redesign. The subflake becomes the flake and the contract does not change. OSF3 · OSF6 · OSF7

OSF3, OSF4, OSF6 and OSF7 are independent siblings under OSF1; OSF5 closes the track. Each phase is a consumer deleting its own OS traversal, independently revertible.

Out of scope, deliberately: foreground process (a PTY-fd fact — tcgetpgrp on the pty, so it stays kaval’s), anything requiring root — OSF6 is the best honest answer without privilege, not an escalation — and any daemon/resident mode. This is a one-shot sampler; if startup cost ever becomes the problem, the answer is to revisit the operational model, not to hide it behind a resident process. The same restraint applies outward: no TUI, no kill, no docker verbs — the broad user-facing surface is what made portls and portview wrong for embedding, and osfacts stays embeddable by staying narrow.
